rejected_summaries.title: One query timeout permanently bricks the connection with no recovery path, and the abandoned DB connection is never closed
rejected_summaries.why:
REFUTED as stated — the claimed user-facing scenario does not occur, verified empirically against the repo's own venv (anyio 4.15.1).

1. "A single query that exceeds its deadline permanently bricks the connection_id" — FALSE. In `run_bounded` (src/universal_db_mcp/services/executor.py:64-65), the driver call runs via `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` inside `anyio.fail_after`. In anyio 4.15.1, `run_sync_in_worker_thread` wraps the `await future` in `CancelScope(shield=not abandon_on_cancel)` (anyio/_backends/_asyncio.py:2675); abandon_on_cancel defaults to False, so the scope is SHIELDED and the deadline cancellation is silently absorbed while the thread runs. When the thread finishes, the result is returned and NO TimeoutError is raised. Reproduced with the real ExecutionService: timeout=0.3s with a 2s query returned the result after 2.01s with no ToolFailure, `_poisoned` stayed empty, and a follow-up call on the same connector succeeded (poisoning is reachable only via narrow paths, see below). So the mainline "query exceeded 30s" path never invokes `_handle_timeout` and never bricks anything — indeed it doesn't even report the timeout (a separate, unclaimed bug: the hard deadline is not enforced for in-flight driver calls at all).

2. "The worker thread that timed out is still live and holding a real DB connection, which is never closed — the connection leaks" — FALSE. `_handle_timeout` (executor.py:67,72) can only run when TimeoutError is raised at an UNshielded await point, which in `run_sync_in_worker_thread` occurs only before the worker is handed the job (limiter-wait/checkpoint before the shield opens). I verified there is no window where the timeout fires while that connector's operation is executing in a worker, so at poison time there is no in-flight abandoned DB connection. Moreover every connector opens a fresh connection per operation and closes it in a `finally` (postgres.py:281→`finally: conn.close()` at 321; sqlite.py:482), so any completing op always cleans up its own connection.

3. What IS accurate (but narrower than the P1 claimed): (a) once poisoned, the connector is bricked until restart — `AppContext.connectors` is only ever written (server.py:62,85,90), never evicted; `MetadataCache.invalidate_connection` (metadata.py:89) is defined but never called; no reconnect tool exists, so the "reconnect or restart" text (executor.py:50) is misleading. (b) Poisoning IS reachable via two narrow paths I confirmed by test: a driver raising a builtin `TimeoutError` subclass is caught by `except TimeoutError` (executor.py:66) and misclassified as a deadline expiry → poison + permanent brick; and a race where the deadline expires while the call is queued behind a saturated anyio default thread pool (40 threads) before the shield opens. (c) The poison-tombstone itself is a deliberate, documented design: the module docstring (executor.py:6-13) states the connection "is marked poisoned and discarded" and that this residual limitation is reported in tool output; "was discarded" is defensible since the connector is never reused, and spec §245's "discard connections whose cancellation/transaction state is uncertain" is reasonably satisfied by never-reuse given per-op connections.

Net: the finding's headline failure mode (one over-deadline query bricks the connection and leaks a DB connection) is factually wrong in this environment; the real residual issues (no eviction + misleading "reconnect" advice on a hard-to-reach path, driver-TimeoutError misclassification) are P2-level quality gaps, not the claimed P1. The genuine production problem in this code is the opposite one: timeouts silently never fire for in-flight driver calls.

rejected_summaries.title: Client-initiated cancellation bypasses poisoning and the cancel hook entirely, allowing an abandoned query and a new query to run concurrently on the same connector
rejected_summaries.why:
REFUTED as stated — the claim's causal chain does not hold in the shipped runtime (anyio==4.15.1, pinned in out/bundle/universal-db-mcp-0.1.0-linux-x86_64-ubuntu24.04-cp312/requirements/runtime.lock line 5, same as the venv).

Key facts:
1. executor.py:65 calls anyio.to_thread.run_sync with the default abandon_on_cancel=False. In anyio this runs the await inside a SHIELDED CancelScope (anyio/_backends/_asyncio.py:2671 `CancelScope(shield=not abandon_on_cancel)`) whose documented semantics are "ignore cancellations in the host task until the operation has completed in the worker thread". Client cancellation (mcp 2.2.0 dispatcher default "interrupt" mode cancels the handler scope, mcp/shared/jsonrpc_dispatcher.py:81-85) is therefore absorbed, NOT propagated immediately.
2. Empirical repro (task cancelled mid-query, exactly simulating notifications/cancelled): the handler blocked until the 3s query finished and then RETURNED ITS RESULT NORMALLY; cancel_current was never called (0 calls); connector not poisoned; peak concurrent executions on the connector = 1. So the executor's finally (executor.py:69-70) releases the limiter only AFTER the worker completes — there is no "limiter released while worker still running", no concurrent reuse of the connector, and no accumulation of abandoned worker threads (the ~40-thread exhaustion scenario is unreachable; workers always finish and return to anyio's idle pool).
3. The "cancel_current interrupts the wrong query" scenario is unreachable: _handle_timeout (executor.py:72) only runs on TimeoutError, and a pure-anyio test proves TimeoutError never surfaces while a driver call is in flight (a 3s job under fail_after(1.0) returned 'ok' at 3.01s; a post-deadline worker exception surfaced as the worker's own ValueError, not TimeoutError). Sync DB drivers never hit anyio checkpoints inside the thread, so fail_after's cancellation never enters the worker. Lines executor.py:66-68 are effectively dead code with this stack.
4. The only literally true fragment — cancel hook not invoked / no poisoning on client cancel — is moot: the query always runs to completion on its own, so the connection state is never uncertain and poisoning would be inappropriate. There is nothing left to clean up when the finally block runs.

Caveat: verification surfaced a DIFFERENT, more severe P1 than the one claimed — the query deadline is not enforced at all (fail_after around the shielded run_sync never interrupts; a 5s query with a 1s deadline returned its result normally; results are returned past the deadline), making cancel_current/poisoning unreachable dead code, the "hard deadline" advertised in executor.py:3-4 and the "timeout ceilings enforced server-side" tool description (server.py:849) false capability claims (spec §295/§65 violation), and there are zero tests covering run_bounded/cancellation (grep of tests/ found none). The reviewer's proposed fix (catch BaseException and run _handle_timeout on cancellation) would not fix that underlying problem either, since the cancellation never arrives until the worker has already finished. Recommend re-scoping the finding to the unenforced-deadline bug rather than the client-cancel/concurrency/thread-leak mechanism described here.

rejected_summaries.title: Empty HTTP bearer token file silently disables authentication (fail-open)
rejected_summaries.why:
The claim's code citations are accurate (/Users/ag-work/Projects/universalDB-MCP/src/universal_db_mcp/__main__.py:110 reads the token with no non-empty check; line 117 compares `auth[7:] != token.value`), and at the pure-Python level the fail-open condition exists (token.value == "" + header value "Bearer " would pass). But the claimed P0 impact — "completely bypassing authentication on the shared HTTP deployment" — is not reachable in the actual runtime, for two independently sufficient reasons I verified by running code:

1. The HTTP server never starts with the pinned runtime. `_serve_http` decorates `server.streamable_http_app()` (an installed `Starlette` instance; mcp 2.2.0's MCPServer.streamable_http_app -> lowlevel Server.streamable_http_app returns `Starlette`) with `@asgi_app.middleware("http")` at __main__.py:114. The venv's starlette is 1.6.0 (transitively required by mcp==2.2.0, which pins only `starlette>=0.48.0` on py3.14 / `>=0.27` below), and Starlette 1.6.0 has only `add_middleware`/`build_middleware_stack` — the `.middleware` decorator was removed. I invoked the real `_serve_http` (imported from src/universal_db_mcp/__main__.py) with an empty token file and an MCPServer instance: it raises `AttributeError: 'Starlette' object has no attribute 'middleware'` before uvicorn.run is ever called. No socket is opened, so there is no server to bypass. (requirements/runtime.in pins only `mcp==2.2.0`; the resolved starlette 1.6.0 satisfies its constraints, so this is the production resolution, not a venv quirk.)

2. Even on a starlette version where the decorator exists, the exploit request cannot be constructed over the wire. The bypass requires a header value that reaches the middleware as exactly `"Bearer "` (so `auth[7:] == ""`). uvicorn's only parser here is h11 (httptools is not installed and mcp requires plain `uvicorn>=0.31.1`, not uvicorn[standard]). I verified with h11 0.16.0 directly: an HTTP/1.1 request with `Authorization: Bearer ` (trailing space) parses to header value `b'Bearer'` — h11 strips trailing OWS, and it also collapses obs-fold continuations to the same stripped result. The stripped value fails `auth.startswith("Bearer ")`, so the middleware returns 401. The middleware-level BYPASS and the wire-level 401 diverge exactly at the parser.

The sub-claims are code-accurate but are hardening gaps, not a P0 bypass: `_check_secret_file_permissions` is applied to connection password files (config.py:228) but not the token file; the comparison uses `!=` rather than `hmac.compare_digest` (only cursors.py:73 uses compare_digest); a missing token file raises a raw FileNotFoundError at __main__.py:110 instead of a clean CONFIG_ERROR. These are P2/P3 robustness items (unreachable in the current runtime anyway, per point 1).

Separately noteworthy (different bug from the one under review): the AttributeError above means the entire HTTP transport is broken with the pinned dependency set — that is a real P1 startup failure, but it is not the claimed auth-bypass finding.

rejected_summaries.title: TOCTOU race between secret-file permission check and read
rejected_summaries.why:
The mechanical pattern is factually present: /Users/ag-work/Projects/universalDB-MCP/src/universal_db_mcp/config.py line 189 does a path-based `path.stat()` in `_check_secret_file_permissions` and line 229 does a separate `p.read_text()`, so the permission check and the read are indeed two distinct path-resolution syscalls. But the claimed production-relevant TOCTOU does not survive scrutiny:

1. Exploitation requires the ability to replace the path between the two calls, i.e. write access to the secret's containing directory (or control of the rotation process). An attacker with directory-write can replace the password file at ANY time — before the check, after the read, or long after startup — with identical effect. The race grants no capability the attacker does not already have, so it is not a security boundary bypass; there is no secret leakage, auth bypass, or privilege escalation resulting from the window itself.

2. The check is inherently point-in-time by design. Its docstring ("Reject secret files readable by group/other") and the spec line (BUILD_UNIVERSAL_DB_MCP_AIRGAPPED.md:231, "Reject unsafe secret-file ownership/permissions where supported") frame it as fail-fast hardening against operator misconfiguration, not a runtime guarantee — a chmod 0o644 one second after startup is equally undetected, and the repo acknowledges this point-in-time semantics by re-checking in the doctor command (src/universal_db_mcp/diagnostics/doctor.py:155-172, explicitly labeled "belt and braces"). Closing the microseconds-wide stat/read window therefore adds no material guarantee over the accepted semantics.

3. The rotation scenario's worst case is the server consuming a freshly rotated secret without the permission validation in a sub-millisecond window at process startup (load_resolved runs once at startup, single-threaded, adjacent statements). The file was already OS-readable in that state; the server reads it as a credential and leaks nothing further.

So: pattern present, but the issue is unreachable as a meaningful attack and the consequence is at most "hardening check skipped in a microsecond window," which is P3 polish at best (the proposed open/fstat/fdopen fix, ideally with O_NOFOLLOW, is a reasonable hardening habit but not a P2). Refuted as a production-relevant finding.

polish_notes.title: Postgres SHOW allowlist accepts any setting name, including file-path settings
polish_notes.detail: validate_show for postgres matches `^SHOW <ident>$` with no value restrictions (sql_guard.py:309-312), so `SHOW data_directory`, `SHOW config_file`, `SHOW hba_file`, `SHOW ssl_key_file` are all permitted through db_validate_query — these disclose server filesystem paths and config locations without any DB privilege. Spec §9 permits validated SHOW but the intent is a tight allowlist ('do not allow every command with those prefixes'). Only SHOW ALL is explicitly blocked.
polish_notes.fix: Deny settings that are known file paths (config_file, hba_file, ident_file, ssl_cert_file, ssl_key_file, ca_file, data_directory, external_pid_file, ...) or invert to a positive allowlist of benign tuning settings.

polish_notes.title: _PLACEHOLDER_OK regex is dead code — parameter tokens are never validated
polish_notes.detail: _PLACEHOLDER_OK (sql_guard.py:120) is defined but never referenced anywhere in src/ (grep confirms only the definition). The guard reports referenced tables but performs no validation that parameter placeholders are well-formed for the dialect; malformed tokens simply fail at the driver. Either wire it into a placeholder check in _walk_validate or delete it.
polish_notes.fix: Delete the unused regex, or add a placeholder audit in _walk_validate that validates each exp.Placeholder token against _PLACEHOLDER_OK and reports the count in GuardResult so db_validate_query can echo it.

polish_notes.title: policy_fingerprint silently depends on an exception fallback to dataclass repr
polish_notes.detail: EffectivePolicy (policy.py:20-41) is a Python dataclass with no .model_dump(), so the json.dumps(policy.model_dump(...)) branch in policy_fingerprint (cursors.py:94-100) always raises AttributeError and the function silently falls back to repr(policy). This works only because repr of the slots dataclass is deterministic within a process, and it embeds reprs of frozensets and compiled regexes — fragile across Python/refactor changes and guaranteed to break cursor/cache scoping silently if the fallback is ever removed. The same fingerprint also scopes the metadata cache (server.py:104).
polish_notes.fix: Implement the fingerprint from dataclasses.asdict with sorted collections explicitly (e.g. sorted(allowed_schemas)) and delete the exception fallback, or make policy_fingerprint raise on non-serializable input so the breakage is loud.

polish_notes.title: Guard test battery misses the bypass classes that actually break the guard
polish_notes.detail: tests/unit/test_sql_guard.py covers DML/DDL/CTE/SELECT-INTO/functions/table-functions/executable-comments, but none of: locking clauses (FOR UPDATE/FOR SHARE — allowed today), Oracle DB links (allowed today when schema-qualified), non-sqlglot dialect engines mssql/db2 (crash today — every FakePolicy in the file defaults to sqlite/postgres/mysql), sqlite main./temp. resolver bypass (allowed today), ClickHouse SETTINGS (allowed today), or pathological nesting (RecursionError). test_security_primitives.py covers cursor identity/connection/tamper/expiry but not the policy-fingerprint mismatch rejection path (cursors.py:89-90).
polish_notes.fix: Add parametrized cases for each of the above to the ALLOWED/DENIED lists, plus a guard smoke test per configured engine type (sqlite, postgres, mysql, oracle, clickhouse, mssql, db2) and a cursor decode test with a mismatched policy fingerprint.

polish_notes.title: db_explain declares a `parameters` argument but never uses it; EXPLAIN-prefix requirement contradicts the tool description
polish_notes.detail: The signature accepts `parameters: list | dict | None = None` (line 904) but the body never passes it to the connector — callers explaining parameterized SQL like 'SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?' get a policy error or a plan for a statement with unbound placeholders. The description says 'Non-executing query plan for validated SQL', yet the handler requires the SQL to literally begin with EXPLAIN (verified live: plain SELECT yields POLICY_VIOLATION 'sqlite EXPLAIN requires: EXPLAIN [QUERY PLAN] <select>'), and spec §8 lists db_explain inputs as 'Validated SQL and parameters'.
polish_notes.fix: Either strip the requirement by letting validate_explain accept a bare read statement (prepending EXPLAIN server-side per dialect) and bind parameters when re-rendering, or remove the parameters argument and document the EXPLAIN-prefix requirement in the tool description and docs/tools.md.

polish_notes.title: db_sample_table drops connector warnings (truncated=true with no explanation) and pagination cursors are not bound to list filters
polish_notes.detail: Two smaller gaps: (1) db_sample_table returns warnings=st["warnings"] only (line 889), discarding outcome.warnings — unlike db_query (line 829) which merges them — so a byte-truncated sample reports truncated=true with no explanatory warning (sqlite even emits a bogus empty-string warning entry in that case). (2) _page cursors bind identity/connection/kind/policy but not the other list arguments, so a cursor issued for db_list_tables with search='acc' can be replayed with search=None or a different schema (still policy-filtered, so no authorization leak, but page semantics and results become inconsistent with the original request).
polish_notes.fix: Merge outcome.warnings into the response in db_sample_table; add the filter inputs (search/schema/kinds) into the cursor payload (or into expect_kind) when encoding/decoding in each listing tool.

polish_notes.title: db_search_metadata: empty connections list silently means 'all connections'; spec's schemas filter missing; audit record lacks connection id
polish_notes.detail: `conn_ids = connections or sorted(app.resolved.keys())` (line 677) treats an explicitly-passed empty list as 'search everything', which is surprising for an API caller intending 'nothing'. The spec §8 input for db_search_metadata includes 'authorized connections/object types/schemas' — there is no schemas parameter. tool_span is opened without connection_id (line 673), so the audit record for a search across specific connections records connection_id=null, weakening the audit trail relative to every other tool.
polish_notes.fix: Validate `if connections is not None and not connections: raise ToolFailure(VALIDATION, ...)`, add an optional schemas filter, and open the span with connection_id=",".join(conn_ids) or log each probed connection to the audit record.

polish_notes.title: Audit timestamps are local-time, second-granular, and non-RFC3339
polish_notes.detail: ts uses time.strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z') (audit.py:46; same format in server.py _now()). Records within the same second cannot be ordered (fsync-fast bursts are common), the %z offset is '+0000' rather than '+00:00', and local time makes cross-host correlation ambiguous — weak for an enterprise audit trail.
polish_notes.fix: Use datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec='milliseconds') (or time.time_ns with a documented field) for monotonic, unambiguous ordering.

polish_notes.title: AuditWriteFailure raised in tool_span's finally replaces the original tool error and escapes as an unconverted exception; the except AuditWriteFailure branch is dead code
polish_notes.detail: app.audit.record is only called in tool_span's finally (server.py:192), so the except AuditWriteFailure: raise at server.py:164-165 can never fire. If record() raises AuditWriteFailure in finally while the body already raised (e.g. a POLICY denial), the AuditWriteFailure replaces the original error and propagates unconverted; the MCP SDK then masks it as a generic UnexpectedToolError, hiding both the real denial and the fact that fail-closed auditing blocked the operation. The operation does fail closed (good), but the failure mode is opaque.
polish_notes.fix: Delete the dead except branch; wrap the audit write in tool_span's finally and convert AuditWriteFailure into ToolFailure(ErrorCategory.AUDIT/AUTHZ, 'operation refused: audit write failed: ...') so the client gets a structured, actionable error.

polish_notes.title: MetadataCache never explicitly closes SQLite connections and re-runs PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL on every get/put
polish_notes.detail: with self._connect() as conn: is a transaction context, not a close (metadata.py:41, 60, 77, 92); connections are only reclaimed by CPython refcount GC, and each call also executes PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL (metadata.py:37), a superfluous statement per cache access. Harmless on CPython but a latent leak on other runtimes and unnecessary I/O in a hot path that also runs under a threading.Lock on the event loop.
polish_notes.fix: Use contextlib.closing(self._connect()) (or a single long-lived connection guarded by the lock) and set WAL once in _init_db.

polish_notes.title: policy_fingerprint silently always uses the repr() fallback, making cache keys hash-randomized and restart-unstable
polish_notes.detail: EffectivePolicy is a @dataclass(slots=True) (policy.py:21) with no model_dump, so json.dumps(policy.model_dump(...)) in policy_fingerprint (cursors.py:97) always raises AttributeError and the except branch uses repr(policy). That repr embeds frozensets whose iteration order is PYTHONHASHSEED-randomized, so the 'policy fingerprint' differs on every process start: previously persisted MetadataCache entries (metadata.py key includes the fingerprint) can never hit after a restart and linger as dead rows until the 10x-TTL cleanup, and the fingerprint's guarantee rests on repr() stability rather than on explicit fields.
polish_notes.fix: Build the fingerprint from explicitly serialized sorted policy fields (e.g. sha256 of json.dumps of a hand-built dict with sorted frozensets) instead of relying on model_dump/repr.

polish_notes.title: Corrupt or incompatible metadata cache file prevents server startup with no recovery
polish_notes.detail: MetadataCache.__init__ runs _init_db eagerly (metadata.py:30-32) during AppContext construction; if the cache file is corrupt, not a SQLite database, or has an incompatible schema, sqlite3.DatabaseError aborts AppContext creation and the whole server fails to start. The cache is disposable, so a corrupt cache should never be fatal.
polish_notes.fix: Catch sqlite3.DatabaseError in _init_db, quarantine/rename the bad file, and recreate it; log a warning to stderr.

polish_notes.title: `with self._open() as conn:` never closes connections (sqlite3 context manager manages transactions, not lifetime)
polish_notes.detail: Every metadata method (lines 203, 220, 229, 281, 348, 365, 378, 409) uses `with self._open() as conn:`; sqlite3.Connection's context manager only commits/rolls back — it does not close. Handles are reclaimed only by CPython refcounting at frame teardown, and an in-flight exception (whose traceback keeps the frame alive) leaves the read-only file handle open until GC. get_table additionally opens 4+ sequential handles per call (line 281 plus list_columns/get_foreign_keys re-open), amplifying open/close churn per request.
polish_notes.fix: Use `with contextlib.closing(self._open()) as conn:` throughout, and have get_table open a single handle and pass it to list_columns/get_foreign_keys via internal helpers instead of re-opening.

polish_notes.title: Relative `database` path fails with raw ValueError "relative path can't be expressed as a file URI"
polish_notes.detail: `self._path.as_uri()[7:]` requires an absolute path; Path.as_uri() raises ValueError for relative ones. Verified: with database='relative-file.db' the file-exists check passes (line 112) and _open raises the raw internal ValueError (via health_check it surfaces as detail="relative path can't be expressed as a file URI"; via execute_query/list_tables it escapes as an unhandled ValueError rather than a sanitized ConnectorError/FileNotFoundError with the artifact-naming message the missing-file path produces).
polish_notes.fix: In __init__, do `self._path = Path(path).resolve()` and reject non-existing/relative configs with the same clear ValueError style used for the missing-file case (raise FileNotFoundError or ConnectorError naming the configured path and connection).

polish_notes.title: list_tables/get_table expose sqlite_schema (and FTS shadow tables) as ordinary user tables
polish_notes.detail: PRAGMA table_list includes sqlite_schema (verified: list_tables returned ('sqlite_schema', None, None)) and shadow tables of virtual tables (kind='shadow', mapped to 'table' at line 240-241). Users listing tables see internal catalog and implementation-detail objects, which also then appear in db_search_metadata and as sample/explain targets.
polish_notes.fix: Skip rows whose name starts with 'sqlite_' (and optionally kind == 'shadow' unless explicitly requested) in list_tables, or tag them so the service layer can filter.

polish_notes.title: PRAGMA authorizer allowlist includes pragmas with write forms (user_version, application_id, journal_mode)
polish_notes.detail: `PRAGMA user_version = N`, `PRAGMA application_id = N`, and `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` are authorized by the authorizer because arg1 matches the read-oriented allowlist entries (lines 55-57). Currently unreachable (sql_guard denies exp.Pragma, query_only=ON, mode=ro file), so this is defense-in-depth erosion only — but the docstring's 'only SELECT-style reads ... everything else denied at the engine API level' claim is not quite true for these names if any future code path reaches the engine without the guard.
polish_notes.fix: Drop user_version, application_id, and journal_mode from _ALLOWED_PRAGMAS (they are not used by any code path), or accept their PRAGMA only when the authorizer's arg2 (value operand) is None, i.e. read form only.

polish_notes.title: driver_helpers type labels: time values labeled 'date', every unrecognized object labeled 'decimal'; open_module names the module as the engine in errors
polish_notes.detail: `_adapt_one` labels datetime.datetime and datetime.date via hasattr checks (line 60-62), so datetime.time (isoformat, no 'year'/'hour'... it has 'hour' — but no 'year') falls through the `hasattr(v,'year') and hasattr(v,'hour')` test and is labeled 'date'. The final fallback (line 64) returns label 'decimal' for any unhandled object — a UUID, IP address, or custom driver type would be reported as 'decimal', misleading the typed column metadata the spec requires. Separately, open_module (line 20) passes module_name as the engine argument to DriverUnavailableError, so the message reads "'pymysql' connector requires..." instead of the engine name ('mysql').
polish_notes.fix: Label by exact class: datetime.datetime -> 'datetime', datetime.date -> 'date', datetime.time -> 'time'; use repr class name or 'text' for unknown objects instead of 'decimal'. In open_module callers (or inside it via a new engine parameter), pass the engine id rather than the module name to DriverUnavailableError.

polish_notes.title: get_statistics reports reltuples = -1 (never-analyzed tables) as row_estimate=-1
polish_notes.detail: list_tables guards with GREATEST(c.reltuples, 0) (postgres.py:160) but get_statistics uses raw reltuples (postgres.py:263, 274); modern PostgreSQL stores -1 for never-analyzed relations, which is truthy, so the tool reports a negative row estimate with source 'catalog_estimate(...)', inconsistent with list_tables and meaningless to consumers.
polish_notes.fix: Mirror the GREATEST guard or map reltuples < 0 to row_estimate=None with source 'unavailable'.

polish_notes.title: Dead, invalid SQL in list_synonyms (references wrong column; result discarded)
polish_notes.detail: list_synonyms builds `SELECT s.name, OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME(s.base_object_name), s.base_object_name FROM sys.synonyms s` (mssql.py:215) — sys.synonyms has base_object_name as the textual object reference, not an object id, so OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME() on it is wrong — and then unconditionally returns [] without executing it. The dead statement will mislead whoever implements Gate C.
polish_notes.fix: Delete the dead SQL and keep the conservative `return []` with a comment, or implement correctly against sys.synonyms (name, schema_id, base_object_name) when verified.

polish_notes.title: Username supplied without password silently connects with empty credentials
polish_notes.detail: _connect only passes the credentials when BOTH username and password are set (db2.py:65-68); otherwise it calls `connect(dsn, "", "")`, silently ignoring a configured username_env whose password_env is missing (which ResolvedConnection would have caught, but a username-only config plus driver-level mismatch produces a confusing auth error instead of a config error). `_dbi_conn()` and `self._conn` (db2.py:44-45, 71-75) are also dead code.
polish_notes.fix: Validate the credential pairing in __init__ (raise ConfigError for username-without-password), delete the unused _dbi_conn helper and _conn slot.

polish_notes.title: get_foreign_keys scans every FK in the database, ignores the schema argument, and returns empty column lists
polish_notes.detail: The query has no schema/table filter (postgres.py:237-242) — every FK in every schema is fetched and parsed, then filtered client-side by table name only (line 245-246), so a same-named table in another schema leaks its FKs into the result; the schema argument is never applied to conrelid's namespace. KeyInfo.columns is always [] (line 252), so the composed get_table() FK detail (base.py:169) lacks the referencing columns entirely — honest-ish but incomplete metadata users will notice.
polish_notes.fix: Filter in SQL: `WHERE contype='f' AND n.nspname = %s AND c.relname = %s` joining pg_class/pg_namespace for conrelid, and expand conkey/confkey (or use pg_get_constraintdef output) to populate columns/ref_columns; also apply the policy schema check for cross-schema refs.

polish_notes.title: Doctor secret-permission double-check can crash with an unhandled exception (exists/stat race)
polish_notes.detail: The belt-and-braces block at doctor.py:156-172 calls `pf.exists()` then `pf.stat()` with no try/except. If the file disappears between the two calls, pf.stat() raises FileNotFoundError and the whole doctor run aborts with a traceback instead of producing its JSON report (run_doctor has no outer guard). The block is also largely redundant: ResolvedConnection (lines 80-84 above) already enforces the same permission rule and reports it as a fatal check. The inline `import sys as _sys` (line 160) is unnecessary since sys is already imported at module top.
polish_notes.fix: Delete the redundant block (the ResolvedConnection check already covers it), or wrap it in try/except OSError and reuse the module-level sys import.

polish_notes.title: Name validators accept non-ASCII/Unicode names (isalnum is Unicode-aware)
polish_notes.detail: resolve_env_name (line 199) uses `name.replace('_', '').isalnum()` and the connection-id validator (line 179) uses `name.replace('-', '').replace('_', '').isalnum()`. Python's str.isalnum() returns True for Unicode letters/digits, so names like 'PASS①WORD' (verified: isalnum -> True) or connection id 'café' pass validation, despite the error messages promising '[A-Za-z0-9_-]'. Unicode env names are effectively unusable/undebuggable and Unicode connection ids leak into cursors, audit records, and error messages where ASCII is assumed.
polish_notes.fix: Use explicit ASCII patterns: env names must match `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`; connection ids must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$`.

polish_notes.title: SQLite connections are not required to declare 'database' at config load
polish_notes.detail: ConnectionConfig._hosts skips the host/database requirement for sqlite (lines 110-114), so a sqlite connection without `database` loads successfully. It only fails later at connector construction (sqlite.py: 'sqlite connection requires database path') surfaced as a generic CONNECTION_ERROR, and doctor reports the odd message "data file '' not found". Every other failure of this shape (missing host/database for remote engines) is a clean load-time ConfigError.
polish_notes.fix: In _hosts, require `self.database` for sqlite as well (a path string); optionally also verify the parent directory exists at load time or leave that to doctor.

polish_notes.title: Envelope docstring documents the wrong binary cell shape
polish_notes.detail: responses.py:13 states binary/LOB data is `{"$binary": "<base64>"}`, but the actual implementation emits `{"$binary_b64": "...", "$truncated": true}` in both driver_helpers.py:58-59 and sqlite.py:92-93, and docs/tools.md:52 correctly documents `$binary_b64`. A client written against the canonical model's docstring would fail to decode blob cells.
polish_notes.fix: Update the responses.py docstring to `"binary/LOB data is {\"$binary_b64\": \"<base64>\"}` (with `\"$truncated\": true` when cut) to match the implementation and docs/tools.md.

polish_notes.title: ErrorCategory is a plain string-constant class; ToolFailure accepts arbitrary category strings
polish_notes.detail: ErrorCategory (responses.py:51-61) is a namespace of string attributes, and ToolFailure.__init__ types `category: str` with no validation (errors.py:17-19). A typo like ErrorCategory.TIMEUT or a raw literal passed by a future caller produces a malformed stable-category prefix that clients matching on 'TIMEOUT:' would silently miss, undermining the 'stable categories' contract in the module docstring. Unlike the CapabilityState StrEnum in capabilities.py, there is no exhaustiveness checking.
polish_notes.fix: Convert ErrorCategory to a StrEnum (mirroring CapabilityState) and type ToolFailure.category as ErrorCategory, so invalid categories fail at construction and mypy can check exhaustiveness.

polish_notes.title: Gate C drifts from the shipped bundle: unpinned clickhouse:latest and client-image dependency versions independent of runtime.lock
polish_notes.detail: The clickhouse fixture uses the floating tag `clickhouse/clickhouse-server:latest` (line 92) while postgres/mysql are pinned to major tags — 'latest' makes Gate C results non-reproducible. The test-client image (lines 24-28) pip-installs hard-coded versions (psycopg 3.3.5, mcp 2.2.0, etc.) on the staging machine from PyPI, which can drift from the versions in the bundle's requirements/runtime.lock, so Gate C does not prove the shipped driver wheels work. The results.json written at lines 125-131 records only the pytest exit code, dropping which fixtures were ready vs blocked, so 'blocked' engines are invisible in machine-readable evidence (spec §14 requires distinguishing blocked/skipped).
polish_notes.fix: Pin the ClickHouse tag to a specific version; build the client image from the bundle's wheelhouse (or assert client-image versions equal the runtime.lock set at run time); write per-fixture status (ready/blocked) into results.json.

polish_notes.title: Egress violation filter exempts all loopback connects and ignores IPv6 address formats
polish_notes.detail: The violation filter (lines 75-78) excludes every connect() to 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0 regardless of port — egress attempted through a localhost-side proxy or local forwarder on an allowed port would not be flagged, weakening Gate D's 'FAILS on any unapproved outbound attempt' contract. Only the IPv4 `sin_addr=inet_addr(...)` string form is matched; IPv6 connects (e.g. ::1 loopback or an IPv6 internal destination) never contain that substring, so any AF_INET6 connect is counted as a violation — a false positive for legitimate IPv6 loopback and a blind spot for policy purposes alike.
polish_notes.fix: Restrict the loopback exemption to the documented local endpoints/ports actually used (e.g. the MCP stdio transport needs none — consider removing the exemption entirely), and parse AF_INET6 sin6_addr values explicitly, exempting only ::1.

polish_notes.title: Release version hard-coded as 0.1.0 in bundle directory name and manifest instead of derived from the built wheel
polish_notes.detail: The bundle directory (line 82) and manifest['release'] (line 188) hard-code "0.1.0" while the actual application wheel name comes from pyproject.toml (also currently 0.1.0). On a version bump, the bundle dir/manifest.release will contradict the delivered universal_db_mcp-<newver>-*.whl, and installers or operators keying off manifest.release (e.g. load_images_offline.sh's default APP_REF built from '0.1.0', line 31) will target the wrong tag. Manifest honesty ('release/version' per spec §11) depends on this field.
polish_notes.fix: Derive the version once from the built wheel filename (wheel_meta of the app wheel) and use it for the output directory name and manifest['release'].

polish_notes.title: systemd Documentation= points at /opt/universal-db-mcp/docs/offline-deployment.md, which the installer never creates
polish_notes.detail: scripts/install_offline.sh creates only $TARGET/venv and prints next steps; it never copies the bundle's docs into /opt/universal-db-mcp. The unit's `Documentation=file:/opt/universal-db-mcp/docs/offline-deployment.md` therefore resolves to a nonexistent file on any real native-mode install.
polish_notes.fix: Either have install_offline.sh copy the bundle's docs/ to $TARGET/docs (matching the bundle layout the runbooks imply), or change the unit's Documentation= to the actual installed location (e.g. file:/opt/universal-db-mcp/docs/... after the copy is added).

polish_notes.title: Doc claims "re-running the script discards the partial venv", but upgrade_offline.sh never cleans up stale venv.new-* directories
polish_notes.detail: docs/offline-upgrade-rollback.md states an interrupted upgrade leaves venv.new-* behind and that re-running the script discards the partial venv and rebuilds. scripts/upgrade_offline.sh:20-27 only creates a new timestamped venv each invocation; there is no removal of prior venv.new-* directories, so interrupted upgrades leak disk space under /opt/universal-db-mcp and the documented recovery behavior does not exist.
polish_notes.fix: Add cleanup at the start of upgrade_offline.sh (e.g. `rm -rf "$TARGET"/venv.new-*` before creating the new one), or correct the doc sentence to say stale partial venvs must be removed manually.

polish_notes.title: Unit omits resource limits and network-online ordering promised by the hardening story (spec §12 mentions resource limits)
polish_notes.detail: The unit has solid sandboxing (ProtectSystem=strict, NoNewPrivileges, CapabilityBoundingSet=) but no MemoryMax/CPUQuota/TasksMax/LimitNOFILE, and orders only After=network.target (connections to databases at startup may race before the network is actually up). Also `After=network.target` without network-online.target is weak for a service that dials remote databases on start.
polish_notes.fix: Add e.g. `Wants=network-online.target` + `After=network-online.target`, and modest defaults like `MemoryMax=1G`, `TasksMax=256`, `LimitNOFILE=8192`; note in docs that administrators should tune them.

polish_notes.title: Module docstring documents binary values as {"$binary": ...} while the implementation and docs/tools.md use {"$binary_b64": ...}
polish_notes.detail: responses.py's docstring says binary/LOB data is `{"$binary": "<base64>"}` truncated per max_cell_bytes, but the actual encoding (connectors/driver_helpers.py:58-59) emits `{"$binary_b64": ...}` with `$truncated: true`, which is what docs/tools.md:52 correctly documents. The stale docstring is the kind of internal drift this repo's truthfulness rules try to prevent.
polish_notes.fix: Update the responses.py docstring to `{"$binary_b64": ...}` / `$truncated` to match driver_helpers.py and docs/tools.md.

polish_notes.title: test_audit_fail_closed contains dead setup and does not prove the fail-closed path in the server wiring
polish_notes.detail: Lines 34-36 construct an AuditLog over a tmp_path subdirectory and immediately overwrite the variable with the /proc one — the first construction is dead code and the tmp_path fixture argument is then unused. The test also never demonstrates that AuditWriteFailure is what the server surfaces (server.py tool_span re-raises AuditWriteFailure at line 183 before generic masking), i.e. that fail-closed audit actually blocks tool calls end-to-end rather than being swallowed.
polish_notes.fix: Delete the dead line; add one test that app.audit configured with fail_closed=True and an unwritable path causes a tool_span-wrapped operation to raise AuditWriteFailure (not a generic INTERNAL error), matching the re-raise ordering in server.py:181-183.

polish_notes.title: Gate B protocol test omits MCP-level cancellation and clean shutdown under an in-flight request
polish_notes.detail: Spec section 14-B requires the no-network protocol test to cover 'cancellation, and clean shutdown'. test_protocol_lifecycle_and_tools covers init/discover/execute/errors but never sends a cancellation notification for an in-flight request nor verifies orderly shutdown while a request is pending — the paths where stdio servers most often hang or leak the event loop.
polish_notes.fix: Extend the anyio test: start a long db_query (recursive CTE fixture or sqlite busy sleep), send the MCP cancellation notification, assert the session returns promptly (bounded wait) and the server process exits cleanly when the context closes (no orphaned subprocess after stdio_client exit).
